name: Battle of Poltava
info: A Russian army under Tsar Peter I defeated a Swedish army commanded by Carl Gustaf Rehnskiöld near Poltava in Ukraine on 8 July 1709, the largest battle of the Great Northern War; the rest of the Swedish army surrendered three days later.

facts.date: 8 July 1709 (28 June in the Swedish calendar)
facts.place: Near the fortress of Poltava on the Vorskla river, in present-day Ukraine
facts.sides: The Russian army under Tsar Peter I, 75,000 to 80,000 men (80,000 in another account of the build-up), against a Swedish army under Field Marshal Carl Gustaf Rehnskiöld, with King Charles XII wounded, which had been reduced to 20,000 soldiers and 34 cannons by the spring
facts.outcome: The Swedes were defeated and fled the field. Charles XII and Ivan Mazepa escaped with about 1,500 men, and the rest of the army surrendered at Perevolochna on 11 July 1709.

t: The Swedish army had shrunk to 20,000 soldiers and 34 cannons by spring 1709, after a campaign through Russian scorched earth and the coldest winter in Europe in over 500 years, while Peter brought 75,000 to 80,000 men.

Charles XII was wounded in the foot on 20 June and could not stand, so Field Marshal Rehnskiöld led the attack, and about a third of the Swedish infantry under Roos was cut off at the redoubts before the main fight began.
Charles and Mazepa escaped to the Ottoman Empire with about 1,500 men, and the surrender at Perevolochna three days later ended the Swedish army as a field force.
dyk: Charles XII spent five years in exile at Bendery in the Ottoman Empire after Poltava, and returned to Sweden only in December 1715.
ev: Charles XII wins early victories in North Zealand and at Narva
Peter I withdraws from Poland and offers to return the occupied Baltic provinces, except Ingria; Charles refuses
The Swedish army of almost 44,000 leaves Saxony for Russia in August
Charles turns south into Ukraine to join Mazepa, and Lewenhaupt loses his supply train at Lesnaya
Charles besieges Poltava from 2 May and is wounded in the foot on 20 June
The Swedes attack the Russian redoubts before dawn and are defeated in the open field
Lewenhaupt surrenders the remaining Swedes at Perevolochna
Charles returns to Sweden in December after five years in the Ottoman Empire

sections.background:
Charles XII led Swedish forces to early victories in North Zealand in summer 1700 and at Narva in November 1700. It took him six years to defeat Augustus II of Saxony-Poland. Peter I withdrew from Poland in the spring of 1706 and offered to return the Baltic provinces that Russia had occupied since 1703, except Ingria, where he had begun to build St. Petersburg. Charles refused, and Peter adopted a scorched-earth policy to deprive the Swedes of supplies. By then Russia was the only member of the original anti-Swedish coalition still fighting.

The Swedish army of almost 44,000 men left Saxony on 22 August 1707, crossed the Vistula on 25 December and took Grodno on 26 January 1708 after the Russians abandoned it. The Russians were occupied with the Bulavin Rebellion of the Don Cossacks, which the Cossack Hetmanate under Ivan Mazepa helped to contain. In July 1708 the Swedes beat Boris Sheremetyev at Holowczyn and reached the Dnieper.

General Lewenhaupt, ordered to bring supplies and about 12,000 men from Courland, left late and joined Charles only on 11 October. Charles then chose to move south into Ukraine to join Mazepa, who had decided to rebel against Peter. Lewenhaupt was attacked at Lesnaya and lost his supply train and half of his force. Aleksandr Menshikov reached Mazepa's headquarters at Baturyn first and ordered the population massacred and the city razed.
sections.forces:
After the Great Frost of 1708 to 1709, called the coldest winter in Europe in over 500 years, Charles was left with 20,000 soldiers and 34 cannons, about half the army's original size. He had been cut off from further help: the Swedish forces under von Krassow in Poland had turned aside to deal with the Sandomierz Confederation. Short of supplies, he laid siege to the fortress of Poltava on 2 May 1709. Peter marched to relieve it with 80,000 men, a figure given elsewhere as 75,000 to 80,000, and built a fortified camp on the Vorskla 4 km north of the town.

On 20 June, while observing the Russian position, Charles was hit in the foot by a stray bullet and could not stand. He gave operational command to Field Marshal Carl Gustaf Rehnskiöld.

The Yakovetski and Budyschenski woods formed a corridor between the armies, which the Russians closed with six forts and four more redoubts, so that the ten works formed a T shape and could give flanking fire. Two redoubts were still unfinished on the morning of the battle. The other eight held 4,000 Russians, with 10,000 cavalry under Menshikov behind them. The Swedish plan was for four columns of infantry and six of cavalry to form during the night 600 metres south of the redoubts and attack before dawn, bypassing them to reach the Russian camp.
sections.course:
The infantry was in place by 2:30 a.m., but the cavalry lost its way and arrived late. Axel Gyllenkrok saw the Russians still working on the two nearest redoubts, and a reconnaissance by Schlippenbach was discovered and the alarm raised by a pistol shot. The surprise was lost and the Swedes lacked cannon to breach the works. After consulting Charles, Carl Piper and Lewenhaupt, Rehnskiöld decided to go on, saying, "In the name of God then, let us go forward". It was nearly 4:00 a.m. on 28 June in the Swedish calendar. Roos's column took the first two redoubts and killed every Russian inside, but by 4:30 its attack on the third had stalled.

Lewenhaupt's ten battalions on the right bypassed the first four redoubts, and Hamilton's cavalry on the left drove back the Russian cavalry. By 5:00 a.m. both wings were past the rear line of redoubts. Rehnskiöld halted the pursuit and ordered Lewenhaupt to withdraw west, where they waited two hours for Roos. Roos had six battalions, a third of the Swedish infantry, and after heavy losses led his remaining 1,500 of 2,600 men into the Yakovetski woods at 6:00 a.m. He was driven to an abandoned fort and surrendered at 9:30 a.m.

Unaware of this, the Swedes were faced by Peter's 42 battalions, 22,000 soldiers, who advanced from the camp with 55 three-pounder cannons and 32 guns on the ramparts. At 9:45 Rehnskiöld ordered the Swedish line forward. The Swedes were on the verge of a breakthrough, but their cavalry had not reformed in time, the left flank threw down its weapons and fled, and the Russians filled the gap. Menshikov's cavalry then attacked the Swedes from the rear.
sections.aftermath:
Charles ordered a retreat to the woods and gathered what troops he could, including the remnants of Creutz's detachment. With his litter destroyed, he rode on horseback and reached his baggage train at Pushkaryovka after 1:00 p.m., when the battle was over. He abandoned the siege of Poltava and retreated south at about 7:00 p.m. Lewenhaupt led the surviving Swedes and some Cossacks to the Dnieper, was pursued by Russian regular cavalry and 3,000 Kalmyk auxiliaries, and surrendered at Perevolochna on 11 July.

The Swedes lost many of their senior officers as prisoners: Field Marshal Rehnskiöld, Major Generals Schlippenbach, Stackelberg and Hamilton, Prince Maximilian Emanuel and Piper. Peter held a banquet in two large tents on the battlefield. Voltaire assumed that his toast to the Swedish generals as masters of war was meant as a message to his own generals about disloyalty. Two mass graves held the Russian dead, 500 metres south-west of the Russian camp. Peter took many Swedes prisoner and sent them to Siberia.

Charles and Mazepa escaped with about 1,500 men to Bendery in Moldavia, then controlled by the Ottoman Empire. Charles spent five years in exile there and returned to Sweden in December 1715. The high vizier was eventually paid off in a tangle of intrigue, which at one point involved a ransom of the Russian crown jewels, according to Charles's prison translator.
sections.sources:
Much of what is known of the day comes from the reports of Swedish officers and a few named witnesses. For the weather, which was very hot and humid with the sun hidden by smoke from the Russian cannon in the fort, the evidence is Charles himself and other Swedish officers. Voltaire is the source for the reason behind Peter's toast, and he only assumed it. The tale of the ransom of the Russian crown jewels comes from Charles's prison translator.

The day is timed to the half hour, from the arrival of the infantry at 2:30 a.m. to Roos's surrender at 9:30 a.m. and the Swedish advance at 9:45, and the date is 8 July 1709 in one calendar and 28 June in the Swedish one. Estimates of the Russian army’s strength run from 75,000 to 80,000. Two mass graves held the Russian dead, 500 metres south-west of their camp.

The battlefield has been listed by Ukraine since 3 September 2009 as a monument of national historical significance.
sections.legacy:
Poltava is called the decisive and largest battle of the Great Northern War and the greatest military catastrophe in Swedish history. It was a turning point in the war in favour of the anti-Swedish coalition, which was revived and attacked the weakened Swedish Empire on several fronts with renewed vigour.

Sweden lost its status as a European great power, and Poltava ended the time in which it was the dominant power in the Baltic region. After the war that position was taken over by the Russian Empire, and the battle also marked the beginning of Russian supremacy in eastern Europe. The battle is of crucial importance in the history of Sweden, Russia and Ukraine alike.

For Mazepa and the Cossack Hetmanate the battle ended the attempt to join Charles against Peter, and Mazepa went into exile with the king. In Sweden the surrender at Perevolochna three days later added to the disaster, since it took the rest of the army, apart from the 1,500 who escaped with the king and Mazepa. Charles returned to Sweden only in December 1715, after five years in exile. Since 2009 Ukraine has listed the battlefield as a monument of national historical significance.

summary: At Poltava on 8 July 1709 a Russian army under Peter I defeated the Swedes under Rehnskiöld, with Charles XII wounded, and the rest of the Swedish army surrendered at Perevolochna three days later. It is called the greatest military catastrophe in Swedish history and the start of Russian supremacy in eastern Europe.
references: Peter Englund, The Battle that Shook Europe: Poltava and the Birth of the Russian Empire (I.B. Tauris, 2003)
Angus Konstam, Poltava 1709: Russia Comes of Age (Osprey, 1994)
Robert K. Massie, Peter the Great: his Life and World (Ballantine Books, 1980)
Michel Glaeser, By Defeating my Enemies: Charles XII of Sweden and Great Northern War (Helion & Company, 2020)
notes: The article gives no casualty figures for either army; the page says so. Do not add any from memory.

Strength: lead says 75,000-80,000 Russians, Prelude says 80,000; I gave both. Swedish strength is the 20,000 and 34 cannons the article gives for spring 1709; it gives no Swedish figure for the day itself. The Russian infantry of 42 battalions is given as 22,000.

The article's sources are thin: it names no chronicler or historian. The sources and legacy sections are therefore built from the few attributions and statements it makes and are short on content; the editor may want to add from a second article. The legacy section's last sentence about the 2009 listing is an inference ('shows the site is still marked') and may be cut.

Dates: the article gives 8 July 1709 in the lead and '28 June (Swedish calendar)' in the Battle section; I did not add the words 'new style' to the article's own text beyond the 'Swedish calendar' label. The sources section says 'new style'; the article does not use that term, so the editor should check or cut it.

The article contradicts itself or is loose in places: the Prelude says Charles had 20,000 soldiers but the Battle section lists 4,000 Swedish infantry facing the Russians in the final stage and Roos's 2,600; the article calls the final phase 'a Cannae variation'; I left that phrase out. 'Previously when defeating Peter, Charles had gone so far as to pay the Russian troops' is unclear and was left out. Charles 'retained his magisterial calm demeanor' was left out as praise.
The statement that Menshikov reached Baturyn first and ordered the massacre is in the article's own voice; it gives no figures.
Left out: Voltaire's full anecdote beyond the toast, the Great Frost as 'extremely harsh', the Kalmyks and Cossacks roaming the plain, and the details of which regiments formed the Russian wings.
